title: Mike Johnson Will Not Seek House Minority Leader Role After Losses
excerpt: The House speaker told staff on Wednesday morning he will not run to lead Republicans in the minority, opening a succession contest after Democrats took control of both the House and the Senate in Tuesday's midterms.
body:
• House Speaker Mike Johnson told staff on Wednesday morning, November 4, that he will not run for House minority leader, according to sources familiar with the announcement cited by USA TODAY and other outlets.
  • Johnson won reelection in his Louisiana district and is not expected to resign from Congress; he is giving up the leadership role, not his seat.
  • House Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan are the likely contenders to succeed him, with House Republicans planning leadership elections on November 10.
  • For readers: Democrats will hold the majority in both chambers when the new Congress takes over in January, and one Senate race, in Mississippi, was still uncalled on Wednesday with Democrat Scott Colom 43 votes ahead.

House Speaker Mike Johnson will not run for minority leader after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections, he told staff on Wednesday morning, November 4, according to two sources familiar with the announcement cited by USA TODAY. The decision is the first leadership consequence of Tuesday's result, which The Videshi reported earlier on Wednesday: Democrats captured both the House and the Senate in a midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump.

Johnson handily won reelection to his Louisiana congressional district, USA TODAY reported. What he is surrendering is the top Republican job in the House. Democrats will be in the majority in the House and the Senate in the next legislative session, and Johnson will not seek to lead his party from the minority.

A reversal from the campaign

The announcement reverses what Johnson had said during the campaign. In a June 29 interview with USA TODAY, he said he intended to remain in charge of House Republicans after the election.

"I intend to win the election and maintain the speakership. We have a lot more to do, and the last two years of the Trump administration will be just as epic as the first two. I intend to keep steady hands at the wheel."

— Mike Johnson, House Speaker, in a June 29 interview with USA TODAY

Johnson is not expected to resign from Congress, a second person familiar with his thinking told USA TODAY, and he had recently told CBS News he intended to remain as leader if Republicans lost the House, News9 reported.

The race to succeed him

Among the likely contenders are fellow Louisiana Representative Steve Scalise, the current majority leader, and Ohio Representative Jim Jordan, the current House Judiciary Committee chairman, USA TODAY reported. A person familiar with the situation said Johnson did not want to get in the way of Scalise's ambitions; Scalise ran for speaker in 2023 but dropped out after failing to consolidate support, after which Johnson became speaker. House Republicans plan to hold their leadership elections on November 10, one week after Election Day, according to a Republican aide cited by News9. CBS News has projected that Democrats will take control of the House in January.

One Senate race still uncalled

While the control of Congress is settled, at least one result from Tuesday was still open on Wednesday morning. In Mississippi, the Senate contest between Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democratic challenger Scott Colom was not decided on Tuesday and was expected to drag on for days, the Mississippi Clarion Ledger reported.

Colom was 43 votes ahead on Wednesday morning, according to CNN figures cited by the Clarion Ledger, with ABC News reporting the same tally. Both Colom and Hyde-Smith stood at 48.9 percent of the vote, and independent Ty Pinkins had 2.1 percent. Around midnight, Colom had held a 28-vote lead. Most Mississippi counties had not reported complete vote totals, and there could be up to 15,000 affidavit ballots still to be counted, according to the Colom campaign, the Clarion Ledger reported. That figure is the campaign's estimate, not a confirmed count.

What happens next

Two dates now structure the transition. House Republicans choose their minority leader on November 10, and Democrats take control of the House in January, when the new Congress convenes. For Indian American readers, the practical consequence is the change in who sets the legislative agenda and chairs the committees that handle immigration, technology and tax policy for the next two years. The Mississippi count, by contrast, will be resolved by election officials as the remaining ballots are tallied, and it does not change which party controls the Senate, a result already established by the wider midterm outcome reported earlier on Wednesday.
